analogy.p: Imagine a long line of people standing shoulder to shoulder. A **P-wave** is like someone pushing the first person: each person shoves the next, so a ripple of squashing and stretching passes along the line in the **same direction as the push**. An **S-wave** is like the people holding hands and the first person flicking their arm up and down: a sideways ripple passes along **because each person is gripped to the next**. If the people let go and wandered about like particles in a liquid, the push would still pass (they still bump into each other) but the sideways flick would not, because there are no grips to pull the neighbour. This analogy breaks down because real rock is three-dimensional, the speeds depend on density and pressure, and real particles do not move along the line as people can.
analogy.t: A crowd doing 'the wave' versus a pushed queue

bullets: **P-waves** are **longitudinal** seismic waves; **S-waves** are **transverse** seismic waves.
**P-waves** travel through **solids and liquids**; **S-waves** travel through **solids only** (they **cannot travel through a liquid**).
P-waves travel **faster** than S-waves, so P-waves are detected **first** (P = primary, the first to arrive; S = secondary).
P-waves and S-waves give evidence for the **structure and size of the Earth's core**.
Earthquakes release energy that is carried away as seismic waves, which are detected by **seismometers**.
Be ready to **link** this to the wave equation, refraction, and the difference between longitudinal and transverse waves (Waves topic).
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA 8463 (Physics only, in the waves topic on detection and exploration) wants you to know that **seismic waves** are produced by **earthquakes**, that there are two types, **P-waves** and **S-waves**, and that the way these waves travel through the Earth gives **evidence for the structure of the Earth, including the size and state of the core**. You must be able to say which type is longitudinal and which is transverse, which can pass through liquids, which travels faster, and what happens at the boundaries between layers. You are then expected to use this to explain why scientists believe the outer core is liquid. Examiners reward precise comparisons, so learn the contrasts as pairs.

bullets: The point underground where the rock slips is called the **focus** (hypocentre); the point on the surface directly above it is the **epicentre**.
The sudden release of **stored strain (elastic) energy** is what makes the waves; the waves **transfer energy** but do not transfer matter over long distances.
Seismic waves can also be made by **volcanic eruptions** and by **explosions** (including controlled ones used by geologists).
The ground shaking people feel is energy from the waves being **absorbed** by buildings and ground.
Seismic waves travel in **three dimensions**, spreading through the whole Earth, and are weaker (lower amplitude) the further they travel because energy spreads out and is absorbed.

**Why it matters:** earthquakes are dangerous, but the waves they create act like a free 'X-ray' of the inside of the Earth, which we cannot reach by drilling (the deepest borehole is only about 12 km, tiny compared with the 6400 km radius).
core.h: Earthquakes: where seismic waves come from
core.p: The Earth's outer layer (the crust and the rigid top part of the mantle) is broken into large **tectonic plates** that move very slowly. Where plates push past or into each other, rock is squeezed and strained, storing **elastic potential energy** like a bent ruler. When the stress becomes too great the rock suddenly breaks or slips along a crack called a **fault**, and the stored energy is released in seconds. Some of that energy is transferred away through the rock as **seismic waves**, which spread out in all directions from the point of the break.

bullets: Longitudinal: vibration direction **parallel** to wave direction (like a push-pull wave along a slinky).
Pattern of **compressions and rarefactions**; the **wavelength** is the distance between two neighbouring compressions.
**Can travel through solids AND liquids** - this is why they can pass through the Earth's liquid outer core.
**Faster** than S-waves in the same material, so they arrive first at a seismometer ('primary').
Typical speed in the crust is of the order of **5 to 8 km/s** (several thousand metres per second).
P-waves slow down when they pass from the solid mantle into the liquid outer core and change direction (**refraction**).
In the same way as sound, the speed depends on how **stiff** and how **dense** the material is.
core.p: **P-waves** are **longitudinal** waves: the particles of the rock vibrate **backwards and forwards parallel to the direction in which the wave is travelling**. This makes regions where the particles are squashed together, called **compressions**, and regions where they are spread apart, called **rarefactions**. Because a P-wave works by pushing and pulling the material, it can travel through any material that can be compressed, so it moves through **solids and liquids** (and gases, such as sound in air).

bullets: Transverse: vibration direction **perpendicular** to wave direction (like a wave on a rope).
**Only travel through solids**; **stopped by liquids** (S-waves are not transmitted through the liquid outer core).
**Slower** than P-waves (roughly 0.6 times the speed of a P-wave in the crust) so they arrive **second** ('secondary').
Usually the more **destructive** at the surface because of larger amplitude and sideways shaking (extra detail, not required for the exam).
S-waves are **absorbed or reflected** at a solid-liquid boundary, which creates a **shadow zone** on the opposite side of the Earth.
Linked idea: a **transverse** wave needs the medium to have **rigidity (a shear strength)**.
core.p: **S-waves** are **transverse** waves: the particles vibrate **at right angles to the direction of travel** (side to side or up and down), making **crests and troughs**. For a transverse wave to travel, each layer of material must be able to pull its neighbour sideways and then spring back, and only a **solid** can do this because the particles are held in fixed positions by strong bonds. A liquid just flows when you try to shear it, so it cannot pass the sideways motion on. That is why **S-waves cannot travel through liquids**.

bullets: **Type of wave:** P = longitudinal; S = transverse.
**Direction of particle vibration:** P = parallel to travel; S = perpendicular to travel.
**Materials:** P = solids **and** liquids; S = solids **only**.
**Speed:** P is **faster** (arrives first); S is slower (arrives second).
**Seismometer record:** P-wave trace appears first, then a bigger S-wave trace some seconds later.
**Behaviour at the outer core:** P-waves **continue but refract** (change speed and direction); S-waves **stop** (are not transmitted).
**Shadow zones:** S-waves have one beyond about **104 degrees** from the epicentre; P-waves have a ring-shaped one between about **104 and 140 degrees**.
Both can be **reflected** and **refracted** at boundaries between layers of different density.
core.h: P-waves and S-waves compared (learn as pairs)
core.p: Exam questions often ask you to compare the two waves or to say which one gives which piece of evidence. The easiest way to revise is to learn them side by side and remember the memory aid 'P = push-pull, passes through everything; S = shake sideways, solids only'. The differences in what each wave can do are the whole reason we can tell what the inside of the Earth is made of.

bullets: **wave speed = frequency x wavelength** (v = f λ), v in m/s, f in hertz (Hz), λ in metres (m).
**distance = speed x time**, so time = distance ÷ speed and speed = distance ÷ time.
Seismic speeds are usually quoted in **km/s**; convert to **m/s** by multiplying by 1000 (8 km/s = 8000 m/s).
Typical seismic frequencies are low (often a fraction of a hertz to a few hertz), so wavelengths are **kilometres long**: e.g. f = 0.5 Hz, v = 8000 m/s gives λ = 16 000 m = 16 km.
Speed generally **increases with depth in the mantle** as rock becomes denser and stiffer under pressure.
Speed changes **suddenly** at boundaries between layers, causing **refraction** and some **reflection**.
P-wave speed **drops sharply** at the mantle-outer core boundary because the material changes from solid mantle to liquid outer core, which is less rigid and has different density.
core.h: Wave speed, and what decides it
core.p: Like all waves, a seismic wave obeys the **wave equation**: wave speed (m/s) = frequency (Hz) x wavelength (m), written v = f x λ. The speed is set by the **medium**, not by the source: stiffer, denser rock generally carries waves faster, so the speed changes as the waves move through different layers. Frequency is fixed by the source (the shaking of the fault), so when the speed changes at a boundary it is the **wavelength** that changes. Distances are found with **distance (m) = speed (m/s) x time (s)**.

bullets: A seismometer is fixed to the ground; an inertial **mass** tends to stay still while the ground moves under it.
The record (**seismogram**) is a graph of **ground movement (amplitude) against time**.
The **first** wiggles are the **P-wave arrival**; the larger, later wiggles are the **S-wave arrival**.
The **time interval between P and S arrival** gets bigger the further the seismometer is from the epicentre (see the travel-time graph).
The **size (amplitude)** of the trace relates to the strength of the shaking at that point.
A worldwide network allows scientists to see **which stations receive S-waves and which do not**, building up the shadow-zone evidence.
Records from **many stations** combined are needed because one station gives only a distance, not a direction.
core.p: Seismic waves are detected using a **seismometer**, an instrument that measures the movement of the ground. A heavy mass is hung or mounted so that it stays almost still while the frame fixed to the ground moves with the shaking. The relative movement between the mass and the frame is recorded as a trace, called a **seismogram**, showing the ground movement against time. There are networks of seismometers all over the world, so the same earthquake is recorded at many different places.

bullets: Measure the **time gap** Δt between the P and S arrivals on the seismogram.
For a distance d: time for P = d ÷ v(P); time for S = d ÷ v(S); so **Δt = d ÷ v(S) − d ÷ v(P)**.
Rearranged: **d = Δt ÷ (1/v(S) − 1/v(P))**.
Draw a **circle** on a map centred on the station with radius d (use the map scale).
Repeat for at least **three stations**; the circles intersect at the **epicentre**.
With only two stations the circles cross at **two points**, so you cannot be sure which is correct; the third station removes this uncertainty.
In real life, speeds change with depth, so scientists use computer models of the Earth for accuracy (not needed for GCSE).
core.p: Because P-waves travel faster than S-waves, the further a station is from the earthquake, the **longer the gap between the P-wave and the S-wave arriving**. If the speeds of the two waves are known, the time gap tells you the distance from the epicentre to that station. One station only tells you the **distance**, which means the epicentre lies somewhere on a **circle** around the station with that radius. Using **three or more stations**, the circles cross at a single point, which is the epicentre (this is called **triangulation** or trilateration).

bullets: **Crust:** thin, solid rock, about 5-70 km thick.
**Mantle:** solid rock that behaves like a very thick, slowly flowing fluid over geological time; about 2900 km thick; **S-waves and P-waves both travel through it**.
**Outer core:** **liquid** iron and nickel; **S-waves cannot pass**, P-waves can (with refraction).
**Inner core:** **solid** iron and nickel, because of the very high pressure; radius roughly 1200 km.
**Whole core radius** about **3500 km**; Earth radius about **6400 km**, so the core is just over half the radius of the Earth.
We **cannot drill** to these depths, so seismic waves are the **main evidence** for the structure.
Scientists use this together with other evidence (the Earth's **magnetic field**, believed to come from the moving liquid metal in the outer core).
core.h: The structure of the Earth (what the waves reveal)
core.p: The Earth is made of layers. The thin **crust** on the outside is solid rock, between about 5 km (under oceans) and 70 km (under mountains) thick. Below it is the **mantle**, which is solid rock that can flow very slowly over millions of years, about 2900 km thick. At the centre is the **core**, made mainly of **iron and nickel**, with a radius of about **3500 km**. The core has two parts: a **liquid outer core** and a **solid inner core** (radius about 1200 km) which stays solid because of the enormous pressure.

bullets: Observation: **no S-waves detected** on the far side of the Earth from the earthquake.
Explanation: S-waves are **transverse** and **cannot travel through liquids**, so they are **absorbed or reflected** at the outer-core boundary.
Conclusion: at least part of the core is **liquid** (the outer core).
The **edge angle** of the shadow zone (about 104 degrees) allows the **radius of the core** to be calculated by geometry and ray paths.
This is the key **'because'** link: *S-wave shadow -> S-waves can't pass liquids -> outer core is liquid*.
Marks are given for **observation + reason + conclusion**; do not just say 'the core is liquid' without the evidence.
core.h: Evidence 1: S-waves and the liquid outer core
core.p: When a large earthquake happens, seismometers on the **opposite side of the Earth** (more than about 104 degrees around the surface from the epicentre) record **no S-waves at all**. This region is called the **S-wave shadow zone**. The S-waves travelling through the mantle reach the **boundary with the outer core** and cannot continue because **S-waves cannot travel through a liquid**. The fact that the shadow is large and has a clear edge shows that the liquid region is a large, central, roughly spherical core, and the angle of the edge can be used to calculate the **size of the core**.

bullets: P-waves are **transmitted but refracted** at the mantle-outer-core boundary because the **speed changes**.
The refraction leaves a **P-wave shadow zone** between roughly **104 and 140 degrees** around the Earth from the epicentre.
On the far side beyond about **140 degrees**, P-waves that went through the core **arrive again**, later than expected.
**Refraction** happens when a wave changes speed at a boundary; the direction change depends on how much the speed changes.
Detailed analysis of P-waves shows a further sudden change inside the core, which is evidence of the **solid inner core**.
Using the **shadow zones from many earthquakes** allows scientists to map the **size of the core** accurately.
Higher tier thinking: explain that P-waves slow down in the liquid, bending towards the normal on entering the core.
core.h: Evidence 2: P-waves, refraction and the P-wave shadow zone
core.p: P-waves **do** pass through the liquid outer core, but their speed **changes suddenly** at the boundary between the mantle and the outer core, so they **refract** (change direction). This bending is sharp enough that P-waves leave the core pointing in new directions, creating a ring-shaped **P-wave shadow zone** roughly between **104 and 140 degrees** from the epicentre where no direct P-waves are detected. Together with the S-wave evidence, the P-wave shadow zone gives information about the **size and state of the core**. Careful analysis of reflected and refracted P-waves also shows that the **innermost part of the core is solid**.

bullets: **Gradual** change of density/stiffness with depth causes **gradual refraction**, producing **curved** ray paths.
**Sudden** change at a boundary (for example mantle to outer core) causes **sudden refraction** (a sharp kink) and some **reflection**.
Curved paths were **a key finding**: if the Earth had uniform properties, rays would travel in straight lines.
Waves that hit a boundary at **90 degrees** (along the normal) are not refracted but still change speed and wavelength.
Reflected waves from the core boundary are also detected, giving extra evidence about boundary depths.
Link: this is the same **refraction** idea as light entering glass: **speed change -> direction change**.
core.h: Why seismic waves follow curved paths
core.p: As well as the sudden changes at layer boundaries, the properties of the rock change **gradually** with depth in the mantle because pressure increases and the rock gets denser and stiffer. This means the wave speed generally **increases with depth**, and a wave gradually changes direction as it travels, like light bending in air of changing density, so seismic ray paths are **curved**, bending back towards the surface. Where there is a sudden change of material, the speed changes suddenly and the ray path has a **sharp bend (refraction)** as well as some **reflection**.

bullets: Artificial seismic waves are used in **oil and gas surveys** and to study **rock structure** (detecting reflections).
Using reflected waves, **depth = (speed x time) ÷ 2**, since the wave travels there and back.
Earthquakes **cannot be predicted** reliably; instead, **buildings are designed to withstand** shaking and **warning systems** give a few seconds' notice.
Seismometers also detect **underground nuclear tests** and monitor volcanoes.
Limitations: models rely on **indirect evidence**; knowledge improved as **more stations and better instruments** were built, showing how scientific understanding develops with **new evidence**.
Evidence is **peer reviewed**, repeated across many earthquakes, and different scientists' data agree, giving confidence.
core.h: Seismic waves for exploration, and limitations
core.p: Geologists also use seismic waves for **exploration** by making their own small waves using **controlled explosions or vibrating trucks** and detecting the **reflections** from rock layers underground. The time it takes for the reflected wave to return tells them how deep the layer is, which helps find oil, gas, and suitable places for tunnels or building foundations. Earthquakes can be monitored and hazards assessed, but they **cannot be predicted accurately**: scientists can say where earthquakes are likely, but not exactly when.

bullets: Link to **longitudinal and transverse waves**: define both and give the particle motion direction relative to wave direction.
Link to **refraction**: wave speed changes -> wavelength changes -> direction may change (frequency unchanged).
Link to **sound** and **ultrasound**: sound is a P-type (longitudinal) wave; ultrasound is also used to image inside objects.
Link to **chemistry (Earth's structure)**: composition of the core (iron and nickel) and the atmosphere's evolution (separate topic).
Calculation skills: **v = f λ** and **distance = speed x time**, including unit conversion km/s to m/s.
Graph skills: read the P and S travel-time graphs, find the time gap at a given distance.
Describe-explain: use 'because' linking evidence to a conclusion.
core.h: Exam links and Higher tier ideas
core.p: This topic links to several others, so examiners often combine it with the wave equation, longitudinal and transverse waves, refraction and the structure of the Earth from chemistry. Practise writing answers that give an **observation**, then a **property of the wave**, then a **conclusion** about the Earth. Higher tier questions may ask you to explain bending of the waves in terms of **speed change**, or to calculate distances or times from speeds.

exam: **State/Name (1 mark):** 'P-waves are longitudinal'; 'S-waves cannot travel through liquids'. Use the exact terms (**longitudinal**, **transverse**, **liquid outer core**).

**Describe the difference between P and S (2 marks):** one mark for **type** (P longitudinal, S transverse) and one for **what they travel through or speed** (S solids only, P solids and liquids; P faster).

**Explain how the evidence shows the outer core is liquid (3-4 marks):** (1) S-waves are **not detected** on the opposite side of the Earth / in the shadow zone; (2) S-waves **cannot travel through liquids**; (3) so they must have been stopped at the boundary with the core; (4) therefore the outer core is **liquid**. Use a 'because' chain.
**P-wave shadow zone (2-3 marks):** P-waves **change speed** at the core boundary, so they **refract**, leaving a region where no direct P-waves arrive.

**Calculation (typically 2-3 marks):** write the equation (**speed = distance ÷ time** or **v = f λ**), convert km to m if needed, substitute, give the answer **with units**. One mark is for the correct unit.
**Epicentre location (3-4 marks):** time difference P-S -> distance from each station -> circles on a map -> **at least three stations** -> intersection point.
**Graph/data questions:** read **time against distance** graphs carefully; the gap between P and S **lines** at a given distance is the time lag; check **units** on each axis (s and km).
**Command words:** 'Describe' = say what happens; 'Explain' = give reasons using 'because'; 'Suggest' = apply knowledge to a new situation; 'Evaluate' = weigh up advantages and limitations.

**Six-mark questions:** plan a short structure: 1) what the waves are, 2) what each wave does at the boundaries, 3) what is observed, 4) the conclusion about the core, 5) mention refraction and the shadow zones.
**Use key phrases** the mark scheme rewards: 'S-waves cannot travel through a liquid', 'P-waves are refracted', 'shadow zone', 'evidence for the structure of the Earth'.
**Avoid** saying 'the waves are blocked by the core' for P-waves; say instead they are **refracted**.

mistakes.r: S-waves cannot pass through the liquid OUTER core; only the outer core is liquid, and the inner core is solid. Say 'liquid outer core'.
mistakes.w: S-waves can't go through the core.

mistakes.r: P-waves CAN travel through liquids and solids; they are refracted (change speed and direction) at the core boundary.
mistakes.w: P-waves can't go through liquids because they are stopped.

mistakes.r: P-waves are LONGITUDINAL; S-waves are TRANSVERSE. Memory aid: P = Push-pull, S = Sideways shake.
mistakes.w: P-waves are transverse and S-waves are longitudinal.

mistakes.r: P-waves are faster so arrive first (primary); S-waves are slower and arrive second.
mistakes.w: S-waves are faster because they are 'secondary'.

mistakes.r: A shadow zone is where a type of wave is NOT detected (no S-waves beyond about 104 degrees; no direct P-waves between about 104 and 140 degrees).
mistakes.w: The shadow zone is where the earthquake is felt most.

mistakes.r: Say the S-wave evidence: S-waves don't travel through it (observation) because liquids can't support transverse waves, so the outer core is liquid. Heat alone earns no mark.
mistakes.w: The core is liquid because it is hot.

mistakes.r: Waves transfer energy, not matter; the rock vibrates about a fixed position.
mistakes.w: Seismic waves move matter from the epicentre to the seismometer.

mistakes.r: Earthquakes cannot be predicted accurately; seismic waves are detected after the earthquake starts and used to study the Earth and locate the epicentre.
mistakes.w: Earthquakes can be predicted using seismic waves.

mistakes.r: One station gives only the distance (a circle). At least three stations are needed so circles intersect at a point.
mistakes.w: One seismometer can find the epicentre.

summary: The specification asks you to know that earthquakes produce two types of seismic wave: P-waves (longitudinal, travel through solids and liquids, faster) and S-waves (transverse, solids only), and that how they travel and refract through the Earth is evidence for the structure and size of the Earth's core, including its liquid outer core. It matters because it is the main way we know what the inside of the Earth is like, and it is a favourite 'explain using evidence' question (Physics only).

terms.d: Waves produced by earthquakes (and explosions) that travel through and over the Earth, carrying energy away from the source.
A sudden shaking of the Earth's surface caused by the release of stored energy when rock suddenly slips along a fault.
A longitudinal seismic wave that travels through solids and liquids and is faster than S-waves, so it arrives first (primary wave).
A transverse seismic wave that travels only through solids and cannot travel through liquids; slower than P-waves (secondary wave).
A wave in which the particles vibrate parallel to the direction of energy transfer, forming compressions and rarefactions.
A wave in which the particles vibrate at right angles to the direction of energy transfer.
The point on the Earth's surface directly above the place where an earthquake begins (the focus).
The point underground where the rock breaks or slips and the earthquake starts.
An instrument used to detect and record ground movement caused by seismic waves.
A region of the Earth's surface where a particular type of seismic wave from an earthquake is not detected.
The change in direction of a wave as it passes from one medium to another because its speed changes.
The thick layer of solid rock between the crust and the core.
The liquid layer of mostly iron and nickel surrounding the inner core; S-waves cannot pass through it.
The solid central part of the Earth, made of iron and nickel, kept solid by very high pressure.
The distance travelled by a wave each second; wave speed = frequency x wavelength.
A region in a longitudinal wave where the particles are squashed closer together.
A region in a longitudinal wave where the particles are spread further apart.
A crack in the Earth's crust where rocks can slip past each other, often the site of an earthquake.

worked.q: A seismometer detects a P-wave and then an S-wave 36 s later. P-waves travel at 8.0 km/s and S-waves at 4.0 km/s in the rock. Calculate how far the seismometer is from the epicentre. (3 marks)
steps: Let the distance be d km. Time for P = d ÷ 8.0; time for S = d ÷ 4.0.
Check: P takes 288 ÷ 8 = 36 s; S takes 288 ÷ 4 = 72 s; difference = 36 s. Correct.

worked.q: A P-wave travels through the mantle at an average speed of 10 km/s for a distance of 2900 km. Calculate the time taken, in seconds and minutes. (2 marks)

worked.ans: Model answer: S-waves are not detected on the far side of the Earth from an earthquake (they have a shadow zone). S-waves are transverse and cannot travel through a liquid. So the S-waves must have been stopped when they reached the core. This shows that the outer core is liquid. P-waves can travel through liquids, but they refract at the boundary because their speed changes, which is why they are also not detected in a ring-shaped shadow zone.
worked.q: Explain how seismic waves provide evidence that the Earth's outer core is liquid. (4 marks)
steps: Observation: seismometers on the opposite side of the Earth from an earthquake detect no S-waves (the S-wave shadow zone).
Property: S-waves are transverse and cannot travel through a liquid.
Link: the S-waves travelling through the mantle must therefore have been stopped (absorbed or reflected) at the boundary with the core.
Support: P-waves are still detected through the core but are refracted because they change speed, so the shadow zone for P-waves is a ring.
